S01.text: From July first, twenty twenty-six, new graduate students in the U.S. can no longer borrow federal Grad PLUS loans. Leah, an illustrative student weeks from her first spring term, has two private offers on her laptop: nine percent fixed, or variable starting lower, at seven point five percent. [curious] How much lower does a variable rate have to start before that risk has been worth it?

takes.asr: From July 1, 2026, new graduate students in the U .S. can no longer borrow federal grad plus loans. Leah, an illustrative student weeks from her first spring term, has two private offers on her laptop, 9 percent fixed or variable starting lower at 7 .5 percent. How much lower does a variable rate have to start before that risk has been worth it?

S02.text: Students already enrolled and borrowing before July twenty twenty-six keep Grad PLUS for up to three more academic years, or for the time left in their program if that is shorter. New students like Leah still have the basic federal loan, a Direct Unsubsidized loan, up to twenty thousand five hundred dollars a year and one hundred thousand dollars total, with higher limits in professional programs like medicine or law. When a program costs more than that after other aid, the rest can come from a private lender, and that's where Leah's two offers come from. Same lender, same amount, two kinds of rate.

takes.asr: Students already enrolled and borrowing before July 2026 keep grad plus for up to three more academic years or for the time left in their program if that is shorter. New students like Leah still have the basic federal loan, a direct unsubsidized loan up to $20 ,500 a year and $100 ,000 total with higher limits in professional programs like medicine or law. When a program costs more than that after other aid, the rest can come from a private lender, and that's where Leah's two offers come from. Same lender, same amount, two kinds of rate.

S03.text: Both are for fifty thousand dollars over ten years, illustrative numbers, not a real lender's offer. The variable loan's first payment is five hundred ninety-three dollars and fifty-one cents, about forty dollars less a month than the fixed six hundred thirty-three dollars and thirty-eight cents. A fixed rate never changes, so neither does the payment. A variable rate follows a market interest rate, so the rate and the payment rise and fall with it, and nobody knows where it goes next. The distance between the two starting rates is what this video calls the head start. Leah's fixed rate is nine percent and her variable rate starts at seven point five percent, so her head start is one point five points. A point here means one percentage point of interest. Real offers differ: a head start can be bigger, smaller, zero, or negative, with the variable rate starting higher.
